Sinim
sī'nim
n. (a distant land named by Isaiah, from which the LORD promises His people shall come — the farthest point of the compass in the prophet's roll-call of the returning)
From Hebrew Siyniym, a plural gentilic of unknown reference. It has been identified with the far east and with a southern district of Egypt; no identification is certain, and the uncertainty is itself part of the effect, since the word functions in the verse as the place beyond the places you can name.

Biblical Definition

Sinim occurs once. Isaiah is in the middle of the Servant songs, and the LORD has just told His Servant that raising up the tribes of Jacob is too small a commission: “I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth” (Isa 49:6). The promise of ingathering that follows sweeps the horizon: “Behold, these shall come from far: and, lo, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim” (Isa 49:12). North, west, and then a name at the edge of the known world. Whether Isaiah meant the Chinese, as many older expositors held, or a remote southern people, the function of the word in the sentence is not in doubt: it is the farthest place, put in to say that no distance is outside the reach of the covenant. The context forbids reading it as a promise about Jewish exiles only. The Servant is given for a covenant of the people and a light to the Gentiles, and Paul and Barnabas quote this very verse at Antioch in Pisidia when they turn to the nations (Act 13:47). Sinim is the Old Testament's way of writing what John saw: a great multitude which no man could number, of all nations and kindreds and people and tongues.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Sinim; in sacred history it is a far country named by Isaiah among the places from which the people of God shall come.

expand to see more

SINIM, n. A distant land named in the forty-ninth chapter of Isaiah.

The prophet says, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim.

The place has not been certainly identified by expositors.

Many of the older writers understood it of the Chinese, at the eastern limit of the world then known.

It stands in the verse for the remotest region, whence the LORD will yet gather his people.

Key Scripture

Isa 49:6 — "And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth."

Isa 49:8 — "Thus saith the LORD, In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee: and I will preserve thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, to establish the earth, to cause to inherit the desolate heritages;"

Isa 49:12 — "Behold, these shall come from far: and, lo, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim."

Rev 7:9 — "After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;"

Modern Corruption

Isaiah's Servant songs are commonly divided among a second and third author writing after the exile, and read as consolation for returning Jews rather than as prophecy of a world-wide salvation. The dictionary holds one Isaiah, and reads the Servant as Christ.

expand to see more

The critical convention assigns Isaiah 40-55 to an anonymous exilic writer and 56-66 to a third hand, chiefly because the chapters address a captivity that lay a century and a half beyond the prophet's lifetime. The reasoning is the same premise applied to Asshur and to Daniel — that specific prediction cannot occur, therefore any text that contains it must postdate its subject. Scripture itself knows nothing of a second or third Isaiah. The New Testament quotes freely from both halves of the book and attributes both to the one prophet: John cites chapter 53 and chapter 6 in adjacent verses and says of both, “Esaias said again” (Joh 12:39). One prophet, one book.

The reduction of the Servant to the nation of Israel, or to the prophet himself, empties the passage in a second way. The Servant is given “for a covenant of the people” (Isa 49:8) — a person who is himself a covenant — and he is a light to the Gentiles that God's salvation may reach the end of the earth. Israel could not be given as a covenant to Israel. The apostles read the verse as fulfilled in Christ and in the mission that followed Him, and Sinim, wherever it lay, is Isaiah's promise that the gospel would not stop at any border a map could draw.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Siyniym (H5515), Sinim; rachoq (H7350), far, distant; 'ebed (H5650), servant; 'or goyim (H216 with H1471), a light to the Gentiles; beriyth (H1285), covenant.

Hebrew Siyniym (H5515) — Sinim; the far land of Isaiah's ingathering.

Hebrew rachoq (H7350) — far off; ‘these shall come from far’.

Hebrew 'ebed (H5650) — servant; the Servant of the LORD in the song.

Hebrew 'or (H216) — light; given for a light to the Gentiles.

Hebrew beriyth (H1285) — covenant; the Servant given as one.

Usage

"“And these from the land of Sinim” — the farthest name in a roll-call of the gathered."

"“A light to the Gentiles” — the commission the ingathering serves."

"“Unto the end of the earth” — the boundary the promise crosses."
